explanation:
## About 4.2 GFLOP/s — just over 2% of peak

Arithmetic intensity first:

```
I = flops / bytes = 2 / 24 = 0.0833 flop/byte
```

Then the two ceilings, and take the lower:

```
memory ceiling  = bandwidth x intensity
                = 50 GB/s x 0.0833 flop/byte
                = 4.17 GFLOP/s

compute ceiling = 200 GFLOP/s
```

4.17 is far below 200, so the kernel is **memory-bound** and 4.17 GFLOP/s is the answer. The machine's arithmetic units will be idle about 98% of the time, and there is nothing you can do in the loop body to change that.

## Machine balance is the number to carry around

Divide the two machine figures:

```
machine balance = 200 GFLOP/s / 50 GB/s = 4 flop/byte
```

That is the break-even intensity. A kernel with **more** than 4 flops per byte can keep the arithmetic units fed and is compute-bound; **less** and it is waiting for memory. daxpy has 0.083, which is roughly fifty times too little.

The modern numbers are brutal and worth knowing: machine balance has been getting worse for decades, because compute throughput has grown much faster than DRAM bandwidth. A current server CPU with AVX-512 and a GPU are both in the 10-50 flop/byte range. Almost nothing in a real application has that much arithmetic per byte.

| Kernel | Intensity | On this machine |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vector copy `y[i]=x[i]` | 0 flop/byte | pure bandwidth |
| daxpy | 0.083 | memory-bound, 4.2 GFLOP/s |
| Dot product | 0.125 | memory-bound |
| Stencil (7-point) | ~0.5 | memory-bound |
| Naive matmul | ~0.25 | memory-bound |
| **Tiled** matmul | ~n/8, grows with tile | **compute-bound** |
| Dense FFT | ~log n | depends |

Note the last comparison. Matrix multiply has `O(n^3)` flops and `O(n^2)` data, so the *arithmetic* is there in abundance — but a naive triple loop re-reads operands from DRAM and throws the intensity away. Tiling does not reduce the flops at all; it increases the intensity by reusing each loaded tile many times before evicting it. That is why tiling is the single most important optimisation in dense linear algebra, and the roofline model is what explains why.

## What this tells you to stop doing

If a kernel is memory-bound, the following will gain you nothing measurable:

- replacing the multiply and add with an FMA
- unrolling the loop
- switching to AVX-512
- using more cores (you are already saturating bandwidth)

and the following might:

- **moving fewer bytes** — single precision instead of double halves the traffic and doubles the ceiling
- **moving them once** — fuse loops so data loaded for one pass is used by the next
- **non-temporal stores** — `y[i]` is written without being read in some kernels, and a streaming store avoids the read-for-ownership that otherwise fetches a line you are about to overwrite entirely. On daxpy that is up to a third of the traffic.
- **a better layout** — struct-of-arrays instead of array-of-structs, so a pass that touches one field does not drag the others along

The first question about any slow kernel is therefore not "how do I make the arithmetic faster" but "which ceiling am I under". Getting that backwards is how people spend a week vectorising something that was waiting for DRAM the whole time.

## Measuring it rather than assuming

```bash
perf stat -e cycles,instructions,cache-misses,LLC-load-misses ./prog

# or go straight for the model
likwid-perfctr -g MEM ./prog         # reports measured bandwidth
```

Intel Advisor and NVIDIA Nsight both plot a measured roofline directly, which puts your kernel as a dot under one of the two ceilings. It is the most useful single picture in performance work.
